label: PER_AXIS_REWARD_NOVELTY
query: Has axis decomposition or per-axis reward feeding been explored in AI alignment or constrained RL literature? Specifically, providing the agent with multi-dimensional reward component vectors rather than scalar totals?
answer:
Yes. ## Conclusion
Yes. In both (i) classic multi-objective RL (MORL) and (ii) newer AI-alignment/RLHF variants, researchers have explicitly treated reward as a *vector of components* rather than a single scalar, and in some cases have used that vector signal directly in the optimization loop instead of immediately collapsing it into a scalar. In constrained/safe RL, a closely related pattern is standard: the agent receives *separate reward and cost signals* (often multiple costs), and algorithms frequently perform *Lagrangian scalarization* internally rather than “reward-engineering” a single scalar reward upfront. (mossalam2016multiobjectivedeepreinforcement pages 1-2, roy2021directbehaviorspecification pages 3-4, zhou2023gradientadaptiveparetooptimization pages 1-2, dineen2025qalignaligningllms pages 2-3)

## 1) Multi-objective RL: reward vectors are a standard formalism
A central, well-established body of work explicitly models per-step reward as a vector with one component per objective in a multi-objective MDP/MOMDP. For example, Mossalam et al. define an MOMDP reward as a vector \(r_t \in \mathbb{R}^n\) with “one for each objective,” contrasting it with the single-objective scalar reward case. (mossalam2016multiobjectivedeepreinforcement pages 1-2)

Many MORL algorithms still *optimize a scalarized utility* derived from that vector (e.g., linear scalarization \(w\cdot V\)), but the environment feedback itself is explicitly multi-dimensional. (mossalam2016multiobjectivedeepreinforcement pages 1-2, yang2019ageneralizedalgorithm pages 2-4, abels2019dynamicweightsin pages 2-3)

### Per-axis feeding vs preference conditioning
A common design in deep MORL is **not** to feed the raw reward vector to the policy as an input, but instead:
- treat the environment reward as vector-valued, and
- condition the policy/value function on a *preference/weight vector* \(w\), which defines how to trade off objectives.

Friedman & Fontaine (2018) are explicit about (a) vector rewards being provided (“every time step, the agent receives a two dimensional reward”) and (b) feeding *weight parameters* to both the policy and the Q-network: \(\pi(s_t, w_i)\) and \(Q(s_t, a_t, w_i)\). They also show scalarization can be applied during replay augmentation via tuples containing \(w^T r_t\), i.e., scalarization occurs inside the learning pipeline rather than requiring a single scalar reward from the environment. (friedman2018generalizingacrossmultiobjective pages 3-6)

Abels et al. (2019) likewise treat the per-step reward \(r_t\) as vector-valued (“each component … corresponds to one objective”), while using architectures that feed a weight input into the value head and apply linear scalarization in learning/targets. (abels2019dynamicweightsin pages 2-3)

Yang et al. (2019) provide a formal separation between vector reward/return and scalar utility: rewards \(r(s,a)\) are vector-valued, and a preference function (often \(\omega^T r\)) maps them to a scalar objective; they also describe approaches that take preferences as input to value approximators. (yang2019ageneralizedalgorithm pages 2-4)

## 2) Constrained/safe RL: separate cost axes are standard; multi-cost vectors are common
In constrained RL (CMDPs), it is standard to separate a primary reward from one or more cost signals (constraints), which is conceptually very close to “axis decomposition.” Roy et al. describe CMDPs as optimizing a reward while respecting constraints “defined by additional cost functions,” explicitly allowing multiple costs \(C_k\) (k=1..K) and constraints \(J_{C_k}(\pi) \le d_k\). (roy2021directbehaviorspecification pages 1-2, roy2021directbehaviorspecification pages 3-4)

A typical algorithmic move is then to **scalarize internally** via a Lagrangian objective
\(L(\pi,\lambda)=J_R(\pi)-\sum_k \lambda_k(J_{C_k}(\pi)-d_k)\)
(or equivalently a per-step shaped reward \(R(s,a)-\sum_k \lambda_k C_k(s,a)\)), which converts a reward+cost vector into a scalar for policy optimization while keeping per-axis bookkeeping in critics/dual variables. (roy2021directbehaviorspecification pages 3-4)

Zhou et al. (2023) explicitly note that CMDP-style constrained RL can feed back “one or multiple cost signals independent of reward,” with constraints limiting the expected sum of each cost—again an explicitly multi-axis feedback view rather than a single scalar total. (zhou2023gradientadaptiveparetooptimization pages 1-2)

Safe RL methods such as WCSAC/distributional safety critic treat a separate cost (safety) signal distinct from reward and use constrained optimization (often Lagrangian) rather than mixing the signals into a single hand-tuned reward; the cited excerpts focus on a single cost dimension but reinforce the standard “separate channels” pattern. (yang2021wcsacworstcasesoft pages 1-2, yang2023safetyconstrainedreinforcementlearning pages 1-4)

## 3) AI alignment / RLHF: increasing use of multi-axis rewards (rubrics, multi-reward alignment)
Historically, RLHF commonly trained a single scalar reward model. Recent alignment work, however, has explicitly pursued *multi-dimensional reward representations* (e.g., helpfulness/harmlessness/honesty; rubric-based criteria) and in some cases uses the resulting reward vector directly.

### Multi-reward / preference-vector framing
Rewards-in-Context (RiC) explicitly represents multiple rewards as a vector \(r=[r_1,\ldots,r_N]^T\) and preferences as a weight vector \(w\) over those rewards. It discusses how multi-objective RLHF (MORLHF) typically uses linear scalarization over \(w\), and proposes conditioning/adaptation mechanisms aimed at handling multiple rewards/preferences more flexibly. (yang2024rewardsincontextmultiobjectivealignment pages 2-3)

### Explicit “vector reward drives update” (closest match to the user’s question)
QA-LIGN (2025) is unusually direct with respect to the user’s “per-axis reward feeding” question: it decomposes constitutional principles into principle-specific evaluations and states that it “pools the multi-axis assessments into a vector reward, and drives the policy update.” (dineen2025qalignaligningllms pages 2-3)

### Rubric-reward RL: critique of scalarization and axis-preserving training
Lan (2026) (ARL-RR/RLRR) explicitly frames “reinforcement learning with rubric rewards” as replacing scalar preference signals with “structured, multi-dimensional” reward vectors, and notes that prior work often “linearly compress[es] these vector rewards into a single scalar” via fixed weightings (scalarization). It then proposes training schemes (alternating optimization over rubric meta-classes) intended to avoid fixed scalarization and preserve reward structure. (lan2603alternatingreinforcementlearning pages 1-2)

## 4) What’s been explored vs what remains less common
The literature supports three distinct patterns:
1. **Vector rewards exist, but are immediately scalarized for control** (classic MORL with \(w^T r\); constrained RL with Lagrangians). (mossalam2016multiobjectivedeepreinforcement pages 1-2, abels2019dynamicweightsin pages 2-3, roy2021directbehaviorspecification pages 3-4)
2. **Policies conditioned on a preference/weight vector** (agent can adapt to different trade-offs; the “axis” is present in the conditioning rather than being directly observed as a reward vector input). (friedman2018generalizingacrossmultiobjective pages 3-6, abels2019dynamicweightsin pages 2-3, yang2019ageneralizedalgorithm pages 2-4)
3. **Axis-preserving alignment signals** (rubric/constitutional multi-axis scoring) where training is explicitly described in terms of vector rewards used for optimization steps, rather than only a single scalar. (dineen2025qalignaligningllms pages 2-3, lan2603alternatingreinforcementlearning pages 1-2)

What appears comparatively *less standard* (at least in the cited evidence) is the specific design “the policy observes the entire reward-component vector as an additional observation channel at each step and uses it for immediate action selection,” as opposed to using vector rewards for learning signals and/or conditioning on weights/preferences. MORL commonly assumes vector rewards from the environment, but most deep MORL methods emphasize preference-conditioning and scalarization rather than directly giving the reward vector as an observation input. (friedman2018generalizingacrossmultiobjective pages 3-6, abels2019dynamicweightsin pages 2-3, mossalam2016multiobjectivedeepreinforcement pages 1-2)

## Summary table
The following table highlights representative examples and whether they match the strong form of “per-axis reward feeding” (vector given directly, not just scalarized).

| Domain | Paper | What is vector-valued | Is vector fed directly to policy? | Where scalarization happens | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MORL | Mossalam 2016 | Reward vector, one component per objective | No | Outer-loop linear scalarization over weight vectors | Learns separate policies/networks for scalarized objectives; classic vector-reward MORL baseline (mossalam2016multiobjectivedeepreinforcement pages 1-2) |
| MORL | Friedman & Fontaine 2018 | Reward vector from environment | Partial — policy and Q are conditioned on weight vector, not raw reward vector | Linear scalarization during replay augmentation / learning | Explicitly feeds reward-parameter or preference weights into policy and value networks (friedman2018generalizingacrossmultiobjective pages 1-3, friedman2018generalizingacrossmultiobjective pages 3-6) |
| MORL | Abels et al. 2019 | Vector-valued reward, each component an objective | Partial — conditioned architecture feeds weight input to Q head | Linear scalarization inside targets/action selection | Designed for dynamic preference changes; weight vector conditions network rather than raw reward vector (abels2019dynamicweightsin pages 2-3) |
| MORL | Yang, Sun & Narasimhan 2019 | Vector rewards and vector returns | Partial — methods condition Q/value approximators on preference vectors | Scalarization by preference function, often linear inner product | Generalized MORL/policy adaptation framing; separates vector reward from scalar utility (yang2019ageneralizedalgorithm pages 2-4) |
| MORL | Lu, Herman & Yu 2023 | Environment reward vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) | Unclear / preference-agnostic in cited excerpt | Vector-reward Q-learning; discusses linear scalarization and reward augmentation | CAPQL is explicitly “vector reward-based”; focus is algorithmic treatment of vector rewards (lu2023multiobjectivereinforcementlearninga pages 1-3, lu2023multiobjectivereinforcementlearning pages 1-3) |
| Constrained RL/CMDP | Roy et al. 2021 | Multiple cost functions / constraint vector plus scalar reward | No | Lagrangian scalarization or manual penalty weighting | CMDP keeps reward and constraint costs separate; contrasts with brittle scalar penalty engineering (roy2021directbehaviorspecification pages 3-4, roy2021directbehaviorspecification pages 1-2) |
| Constrained RL/CMDP | Zhou et al. 2023 (GCPO) | One or multiple cost signals independent of reward | No | Pareto-style multi-objective optimization with explicit constraint handling | Treats CRL as multi-objective; reward and costs remain separate signals (zhou2023gradientadaptiveparetooptimization pages 1-2) |
| Constrained RL/CMDP | Yang et al. 2021/2023 (WCSAC / distributional safety critic) | Separate reward and safety-cost signal | No | Lagrangian-style constrained optimization; cost distribution/CVaR for safety | Safe RL standard pattern: reward and safety cost are separate, but usually single-cost rather than full reward vector to policy (yang2023safetyconstrainedreinforcementlearning pages 1-4, yang2021wcsacworstcasesoft pages 1-2) |
| Constrained RL/CMDP | Parnika et al. 2021 | Multiple penalty costs plus main cost | Partial — separate critics for penalties, not direct policy input as vector | Lagrangian combination of main and penalty costs | Multi-constraint setup with specialized penalty critics and learned multipliers (parnika2021attentionactorcriticalgorithm pages 15-18) |
| Alignment / RLHF | RiC 2024 | Reward-model output vector and preference weight vector | Partial — model is conditioned on multiple rewards in prompt context / preference-to-reward mapping | Preference-weighted multi-objective handling; avoids heavy RL scalarization pipeline | Explicit multi-reward alignment of foundation models with dynamic preference adjustment (yang2024rewardsincontextmultiobjectivealignment pages 2-3) |
| Alignment / RLHF | QA-LIGN 2025 | Multi-axis constitutional/rubric score vector | Yes | None in the quoted description; vector reward drives update directly | Pools multi-axis assessments into a vector reward and uses it to drive policy update (dineen2025qalignaligningllms pages 2-3) |
| Alignment / RLHF | ARL-RR 2026 | Rubric reward vector / contextual multi-dimensional scores | No | Prior work uses fixed linear scalarization; ARL-RR uses alternating optimization over meta-classes | Explicit critique of collapsing rubric vectors to scalar rewards; preserves structure by alternating over reward axes/meta-classes (lan2603alternatingreinforcementlearning pages 10-12, lan2603alternatingreinforcementlearning pages 1-2) |


*Table: This table summarizes representative work across multi-objective RL, constrained RL, and alignment that uses vector-valued rewards or separate reward/cost axes. It highlights whether the vector is given directly to the policy versus scalarized internally or replaced by preference-weight conditioning.*
